title: Finding a column
prompt:
This is the `patients` data frame. Each row is one patient; each column
is one thing measured about them.

Click the column that holds each patient's systolic blood pressure.
hint:
Column names in R tend to be short. What would you abbreviate "systolic
blood pressure" to?

options.feedback:
Right. And look at what's in it: the same four readings you've worked
with for two modules, missing value included. A column in a data frame is just
a vector — everything you learned in modules 5 and 6 still works on
it.

That's each patient's age. The blood pressures are the column with
one missing value in it.

That's blood type — a character column, since `"A+"` isn't a number.
You're looking for numbers in the 100s.

That's a logical column: TRUE if the patient has gone home, FALSE if
not. You're looking for numbers.

title: Spot the missing value
prompt: One blood pressure was never taken. Click the missing value.
hint: R shows a missing value the same way in a table as it did in a vector.

response.other: That one's a real value. Look for the missing value — R shows it as `NA`.

options.feedback:
Right — row 3, the 71-year-old. Reading across a row tells you
everything about one patient: 71, B+, blood pressure unknown, still
in hospital. Reading down a column tells you one thing about
everybody.

title: Columns that don't line up
prompt:
There are five ages but only four blood pressures. What happens?

```r
age <- c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62)
sbp <- c(142, 118, 131, 156)
data.frame(age, sbp)
```
hint: Each row is one patient. Which patient would the fifth age belong to?

options.text: An error — the columns have different lengths
options.feedback:
Right. Every row is one patient, so every column has to have exactly
one value per patient. With four readings for five people, R can't
know which patient is missing one — so it refuses.

This is the loud, cheap kind of error. The dangerous version is the
one where the lengths *do* match but the values are in the wrong
order, and nothing tells you.

options.text: A table with `NA` added for the fifth blood pressure
options.feedback:
That would mean R guessing that the *last* patient is the one
without a reading. It won't guess. For all it knows, the missing reading belongs to patient 2.

options.text: A table of four patients, with the last age dropped
options.feedback:
R never silently throws away data here. It stops and tells you the
two columns don't match.

title: Pulling out one column
prompt:
`$` pulls one column out of a data frame. Write the data frame's name,
then `$`, then the column's name.

Get the blood pressure column from `patients`.

From here on, the data frames in this module are in the **Data** panel at
the top of the page. Open it to keep `patients` in view while you work.
hint: The column name is exactly as it appears at the top of the table.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
What comes back is an ordinary vector — `142 118 NA 131 156`. So
everything you know about vectors now works on a column: arithmetic,
`mean()`, `is.na()`, filtering with square brackets.

checks.on_fail:
That isn't the blood pressure column. Check the name against the
table.

misconceptions.feedback:
You got `NULL` — nothing at all — and no error. `$` with a name that
doesn't exist quietly returns nothing, so a single wrong letter or
capital slips through without complaint. Column names are exact,
the same way variable names are.

title: Averaging a column
prompt: Get the average blood pressure across the patients who have a reading.
hint:
It's the same as averaging a vector that's missing a value — you did exactly
this in the last module.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
`patients$sbp` is a vector with a missing value in it, so everything from the
last module applies: without `na.rm = TRUE`, one missing reading makes
the whole average `NA`.

checks.on_fail: Not 136.75 yet. The column has a missing value in it.

misconceptions.feedback:
`NA` — the missing blood pressure is still being included. A column
with a missing value behaves exactly like the vectors in the last module.

title: How many went home?
prompt:
The `discharged` column is TRUE for patients who have gone home. Count
how many have.
hint:
A column of TRUEs and FALSEs is exactly what you counted in modules 5
and 6.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
Read it inside out. `patients$discharged` asks *who has gone home?*
and answers `TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE TRUE`. Wrapping `sum()` around it
asks *what's the total number (who've gone home)?* — the brackets in
that question sit exactly where they sit in the code. Since each TRUE
counts as 1, the answer is 3.

checks.on_fail: Not 3 yet. You want a function that adds up the TRUEs.

misconceptions.feedback:
`length()` gives 5 — the number of patients, not the number who went
home. You want to add up the TRUEs.

title: Reading str()
prompt:
`str()` shows the *structure* of a data frame. This is what it gives for
`patients`:

```
'data.frame':	5 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ age       : num  67 54 71 48 62
 $ blood_type: chr  "A+" "O-" "B+" "O+" ...
 $ sbp       : num  142 118 NA 131 156
 $ discharged: logi  TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE TRUE
```

How many patients are in the data?
hint:
"obs." is short for observations. In this data, each observation is a
patient.

options.feedback:
Right. The first line gives you the shape: 5 observations (rows)
and 4 variables (columns). Then each line after it is one column,
with its type — `num`, `chr` or `logi`, which are numeric,
character and logical — and its first few values.

That type column is what makes `str()` worth reaching for, as the
next exercise shows.

4 is the number of *variables* — the columns. Observations are the
rows, and there are 5.

That's 5 × 4, the total number of values in the table. The number of
patients is the number of rows.

title: What the spreadsheet view hides
prompt:
A lab export arrives as `labs`. Opened in a viewer, the CRP column looks
like a column of numbers. `str()` says:

```
'data.frame':	5 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ age: num  67 54 71 48 62
 $ crp: chr  "12.4" "<5" "31.0" "8.2" ...
 $ wbc: num  11.2 7.8 14.1 9 6.5
```

Which column will cause trouble when you use the `mean()` function on
it?
hint: Look at the three letters after each colon.

options.feedback:
Right — it's `chr`, character, because of that `"<5"`. One value that
isn't a plain number turned the whole column into text, exactly as in
module 5.

Here's the part worth remembering. In a spreadsheet-style viewer,
`12.4` and `"12.4"` look identical. You could scroll through this data
and never see a problem. `str()` shows you what R actually thinks
each column is, which is why it's worth a glance whenever you meet a
new dataset or an analysis gives you something odd.
`age` is `num` — numeric — so it will average fine.

`wbc` is `num`. Notice it shows `9` rather than `9.0`; R drops a
trailing zero, but the value is the same number.

options.text: None — they all look like numbers
options.feedback:
They *look* like numbers, which is exactly the trap. Check the type
after each colon: one of them isn't `num`.

title: Converting the column
prompt:
Convert the `crp` column to numbers, storing the result back in the same
column. The second line then checks its type.

`labs` is in the **Data** panel if you want it in view.
hint:
`as.numeric()` converts text to numbers. What goes inside it is the
column itself, `labs$crp`.

solution.why:
The column is numeric now, and the old text version is gone — storing
back into the same name overwrites it.

Look at the warning, though. `"<5"` couldn't be read as a number, so
it became `NA`. That's a real decision, and R just made it for you.
But "<5" doesn't mean nobody knows — it means below 5. Whether it
should be `NA`, 5, or something else is a clinical call, and it's
yours to make.

checks.on_fail:
The column isn't numeric yet. Put `as.numeric()` around the column on
the right of the arrow.

misconceptions.feedback:
`crp` isn't a variable of its own — it's a column that lives inside
`labs`, so R can't find it by that name alone. Pulling a column out
with `$` doesn't create a new variable; each time you want the
column, you reach into the data frame for it: `labs$crp`.

There's a `crp` here without `labs$` in front of it. `crp` isn't a
variable of its own — it's a column that lives inside `labs`.
Pulling a column out with `$` doesn't create a new variable; each
time you want the column, you reach into the data frame for it:
`labs$crp`.

Still character. Whatever is on the right of the arrow has to convert
the column, not just copy it.

title: Reading summary()
prompt:
`summary()` gives a quick overview. Here's what it shows for the blood
pressure column, `summary(patients$sbp)`:

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's
  118.0   127.8   136.5   136.8   145.5   156.0       1
```

How many blood pressure readings are missing?
hint: One of those labels is about missing values.

options.feedback:
Right — `NA's` counts the missing values.

It's worth knowing because `summary()` works on a whole data frame
too. Give it `patients` instead of one column, and you get this
overview for every column at once, including how many values are
missing in each. Real datasets have dozens of columns, so that's how
you spot the missing values across all of them in one go.
Look at the last label, `NA's`. It isn't zero.

There are five patients, but only one of them is missing a reading.
The `NA's` entry counts just the missing ones.

title: The ages of those who went home
prompt: Get the ages of the patients who have been discharged.
hint:
Square brackets keep the values that line up with a TRUE. Which column is
already TRUE for exactly the patients you want?
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
`patients$discharged` is already TRUE for exactly the patients who
went home, so you don't need to ask a question — the column *is* the
answer. Square brackets keep the ages lined up with each TRUE.

You've just used one column to filter another. Because every row is
one patient, the values line up, and that's what makes a data frame
more than a pile of separate vectors.

checks.on_fail:
Not the three discharged patients' ages yet. The blank needs a
column that's TRUE for the right patients.

misconceptions.feedback:
`discharged` only exists as a column inside `patients`. Write
`patients$discharged` so R knows where to find it.

`discharged` only exists inside `patients`. Write `patients$discharged`
so R knows where to find it.
